instagram_caption:
🚨 How a $45.6B private startup crashed into the credit card giants — and what it cost investors and shoppers.

From the mid‑2000s to the pandemic years, buy‑now‑pay‑later companies looked like the next payments superpower. Klarna and Affirm went from near‑zero to headline valuations: Klarna’s private valuation peaked at $45.6B in 2021, and Affirm’s market cap topped roughly $40B after its 2020 IPO. Those weren’t guesses — those were real, jaw‑dropping numbers that rewrote expectations about short‑term consumer credit.

But 2022 changed the math. Higher interest rates, worse-than-expected credit performance for BNPL portfolios, and rising regulatory scrutiny in the EU, UK and US slammed the brakes. By 2023 Klarna’s reported valuation had been cut to around $6.7B in a widely covered down‑round, and Affirm’s market cap collapsed from its peak to single‑digit billions. That’s the “crush” in the visualization: a vertical fall that came as fast as the ascent.

Meanwhile, Visa and Mastercard didn’t flash or crash — they grew. Visa climbed from tens of billions in market cap in the 2000s to several hundred billion by the 2020s as global card transactions kept expanding. Those steady compounding gains are what dominates the right side of the race: quiet, massive scale versus volatile start‑up hype.

This chart race isn’t about rooting for incumbents or startups. It’s about scale, risk and timing. BNPL rewired checkout psychology and pushed competitors and regulators to adapt — but the market also punished models that relied on cheap capital and loose underwriting.

Which side are you on — team convenience (BNPL) or team predictability (cards)? Drop your take: would you use BNPL for a $2,000 purchase? Tell me why.

Title: The BNPL Crash & Card Comeback — a timeline of boom, bust, and stability.

This visualization traces two parallel payment worlds. On one side, Klarna and Affirm exploded from small startups into multi‑billion dollar names (Klarna reached a widely reported private valuation of $45.6 billion in 2021; Affirm’s market cap topped near $40 billion after its 2020 IPO). On the other, Visa and Mastercard continued steady expansion, growing from tens of billions in market value in the 2000s to several hundred billions by the early 2020s.

The turning point came in 2022–2023: macroeconomic headwinds, rising interest rates, regulatory scrutiny in multiple jurisdictions, and weakening BNPL credit performance produced dramatic markdowns. Klarna’s valuation fell to approximately $6.7 billion in 2023 in a well‑publicized down‑round; Affirm’s market cap likewise shrank from its pandemic peak.

The result is a dramatic chart race: BNPL’s lightning ascent and subsequent collapse contrasted with the slow, dominating growth of legacy card networks. The lesson is structural — scale and regulatory resilience often outlast hype.

Sources include SEC filings (Affirm), public company annual reports (Visa, Mastercard), and major reporting from Reuters, Financial Times and CNBC on Klarna’s funding rounds and valuation adjustments.
